subject: Economics
description: Demand-pull, cost-push, stagflation, hyperinflation, deflation, CPI vs WPI

questions.stem: INFLATION caused by RISING DEMAND in the economy is called:
questions.explanation: DEMAND-PULL INFLATION — 'too much money chasing too few goods'. Demand exceeds supply at current prices → prices rise. Causes: govt. spending, low interest rates, increased credit, expansion of money supply, consumer optimism. COST-PUSH INFLATION — input costs (oil, wages, raw materials) rise → producers pass costs on. STAGFLATION — high inflation + low growth + high unemployment (rare; 1970s OPEC oil shocks). HYPERINFLATION — extreme: Weimar Germany (1923), Zimbabwe (2008 — 79.6 BILLION % monthly!), Venezuela (recent).

questions.stem: Inflation in India is officially measured by:

options.option_text: Only the WPI (Wholesale Price Index) used
GDP deflator alone is the official measure

questions.explanation: India's inflation: from 2014, RBI uses CPI (Combined: rural + urban, ~46% food weightage; published by NSO/MoSPI). Earlier WPI (with very different weights — manufactured goods 64%, primary goods 22%, fuel 14%) was the main reference. WPI still tracked but CPI is the policy benchmark. CPI BASKET in India: Food + Beverages 46%, Housing 10%, Fuel + Light 7%, Clothing 7%, Health 6%, Education 4%, Pan + Tobacco 2%, Misc + Recreation. UPDATED periodically (current base 2012=100; revision in progress to 2024).

options.option_text: Stable, zero inflation always for some periods
Rising prices in only one sector of economy

questions.explanation: DEFLATION — sustained DECREASE in general price level (inflation rate < 0). DISINFLATION = decrease in inflation RATE (rate still positive but smaller). REFLATION = bringing economy out of deflation back to normal. Why deflation is bad: consumers postpone purchases (waiting for cheaper prices) → demand falls → producers cut output / jobs → economy contracts (deflationary spiral). Japan suffered deflation 1990s-2010s ('Lost Decades'). Distractor 1 = disinflation. Distractor 3 = price stability.

questions.stem: CORE INFLATION typically excludes which categories?
questions.explanation: CORE INFLATION = headline inflation EXCLUDING food + fuel (the most volatile categories). Why exclude: food (weather, seasonality) + fuel (oil prices, geopolitical events) are highly variable, can mask underlying trend. Core inflation reveals UNDERLYING price pressure — better signal for monetary policy. Persistent high core inflation = entrenched inflation, harder to control. RBI looks at both headline + core CPI. (Some economists prefer 'sticky CPI' or 'trimmed mean CPI' — different ways to filter volatile components.)

options.option_text: Lenders and savers benefit most from inflation
Pensioners on fixed income gain from inflation
Salaried employees with no salary rise also gain

questions.explanation: Inflation effects: BENEFITS BORROWERS — they repay loans in money worth less than at borrowing time (real value of loan eroded). HURTS LENDERS + SAVERS — interest income may not keep up with inflation; real returns fall (especially fixed-deposit holders with rate < inflation). HURTS PENSIONERS + fixed-income earners — purchasing power of pension declines. HURTS salaried (without inflation-linked increments). REAL ESTATE + GOLD often gain (inflation hedges). EQUITY can be a hedge over LONG term (stocks of companies with pricing power).

questions.explanation: STAGFLATION = STAGnation (low or zero growth, high unemployment) + inFLATION (rising prices). Term coined by Iain Macleod (UK Chancellor) in 1965. RARE but very dangerous: standard Keynesian tools (rate cuts to boost growth) WORSEN inflation; tools to cut inflation (rate hikes) WORSEN unemployment. Famous case: 1973-75 OIL SHOCK — OPEC quadrupled oil prices → cost-push inflation + recession in West. India in 2010-13 saw mild stagflationary tendencies. Distractor 4 = recession + deflation = depression.

questions.stem: HYPERINFLATION is generally defined as inflation rate exceeding:
questions.explanation: HYPERINFLATION — extreme inflation, typically defined (Cagan, 1956) as > 50% PER MONTH (~129× per year compounded). Famous cases: HUNGARY 1946 (inflation rate 4.19 × 10¹⁶% per month — worst ever; pengő replaced with forint at ratio 1 forint = 4 × 10²⁹ pengő). WEIMAR GERMANY 1923 (~30,000% per month; price doubled every ~3.7 days; people burning Marks for fuel cheaper than firewood). ZIMBABWE 2008 (89.7 sextillion % year-on-year peak; printed 100 trillion-dollar notes). VENEZUELA 2018 (~1,000,000% annual). Causes: usually massive money printing to cover deficit during crisis. Cure: replace currency, anchor to hard currency or gold.
